title: Statistics - Lesson 10: Statistical Report and Probability Critique Assessment
description: Checkpoint assessment on critiquing statistical reports and solving related probability questions.

questions.question: A report claims, "The new reading app helps Grade 10 students." It studied 16 students who volunteered to use the app. Which question should be asked first?
options: Were the 16 volunteers representative of Grade 10 students?
Did the app use bright colors?
Can the claim be rewritten without numbers?
Was the report printed on paper?
questions.explanation: The claim describes Grade 10 students broadly, so the sample's representativeness matters.

questions.question: Use the table: 20 students chose sports day, 15 chose arts day, and 5 chose academic day. Which statement is accurate?
options: Most students chose sports day.
Half of the surveyed students chose sports day.
All students chose sports day.
Sports day had fewer votes than arts day.
questions.explanation: The total is 40 students, and 20/40 = 1/2. Half chose sports day, but "most" would mean more than half.

questions.question: In a group of 75 students, 45 passed a diagnostic test. What percent passed? Enter a percent.
A probability question says, "Given that a student attended review, what is the chance the student passed?" Which denominator should be used?
options: The number of students who attended review
The number of students who passed
The number of students who failed
The number of students in the entire school
questions.explanation: "Given that a student attended review" restricts the denominator to students who attended review.

questions.question: A sample can be biased even if every percent in the report was calculated correctly.
questions.explanation: Correct arithmetic does not fix a sample that does not fairly represent the population.

questions.question: A graph shows snack sales but does not label the vertical axis. What is the best critique?
options: The graph is hard to interpret because the units or scale are unclear.
The graph is always correct if the bars are colorful.
The graph must be converted into a circle equation.
The missing axis label proves the data are fake.
questions.explanation: Missing labels make it unclear what the values represent, even if the data might be real.

questions.question: A table shows 18 students joined a club and 42 did not. What is the probability that a randomly selected student did NOT join a club as a simplified fraction?
questions.explanation: The total is 18 + 42 = 60. The probability is 42/60, which simplifies to 7/10.

questions.question: Use this two-way table: 12 boys and 18 girls chose rice meal; 8 boys and 12 girls chose sandwich. What is P(rice meal | girl)?
questions.explanation: Among girls, the denominator is 18 + 12 = 30. Girls who chose rice meal = 18, so the probability is 18/30.

questions.question: A headline says, "Students hate the new schedule." The data show 11 of 40 surveyed students disliked it. Which replacement headline is fairest?
options: In the survey, 11 of 40 students disliked the new schedule.
All students dislike the schedule.
The schedule failed completely.
No students like the schedule.
questions.explanation: The fair headline states the actual result and keeps the claim limited to the survey.

questions.question: If a category is the largest single category, it must be more than half of the total.
questions.explanation: The largest category can still be less than half when there are three or more categories.

questions.question: A report gives a probability of 0.25 for choosing arts day. Which statement has the same meaning?
options: The probability is 25%, or 1/4.
The probability is 2.5%.
The probability is 25 out of every 25.
The event is impossible.

questions.question: A survey of 20 student council members finds that 17 support a new campus project. The report says, "Grade 10 students support the project." Explain one strength and one limitation of the report.
questions.correctAnswer: A strength is that 17 out of 20 student council members is a clear majority in the surveyed group. A limitation is that student council members may not represent all Grade 10 students, so the broader claim needs more evidence.
questions.explanation: A good answer should recognize the strong result within the sample while questioning whether the sample represents the full population.

questions.question: A graph compares 92% and 95%, but the axis starts at 90% and the title says, "One section is far better." Write a two-sentence critique.
questions.correctAnswer: The real difference is only 3 percentage points, so the title may exaggerate the result. Starting the axis at 90% can make the difference look much larger than it is.
questions.explanation: The critique should mention both the small numerical difference and the misleading effect of the truncated axis or exaggerated title.

questions.question: Use this result: Among 36 students who attended review, 27 passed the quiz. Write the conditional probability and interpret it in context.
questions.correctAnswer: P(passed | attended review) = 27/36 = 3/4 = 75%. Among students who attended review, 75% passed the quiz.
questions.explanation: The condition is attending review, so the denominator is 36 and the result should be interpreted for that group.

questions.question: A report says, "The data prove the new homework policy works for every student," after 28 of 35 surveyed students improved. Write a fairer evidence-based conclusion.
questions.correctAnswer: In the surveyed group, 28 of 35 students, or 80%, improved after the new homework policy. This suggests the policy may help, but it does not prove that it works for every student.
questions.explanation: A fair conclusion includes the statistic, names the surveyed group, and avoids overgeneralizing to every student.
